thesis: A name still trading above its 200-day average that prints a fresh RSI(14)<30 reading is absorbing short-horizon, sentiment-driven selling (an earnings wobble, a sector rotation, a macro scare) on top of intact longer-horizon demand -- not a repricing of the business. The counterparty is short-term momentum sellers and forced sellers (stop cascades, vol-targeting funds cutting exposure into the drawdown) selling at peak discomfort; the trade is that once that flow exhausts, the buyers already accumulating the name near its 200dma step back in and close the gap. RSI(14) crossing back above 50 is the empirical marker that the flow has turned (median 9 sessions in-sample), which is why the exit is a rule rather than a fixed target -- the thesis is about waiting for evidence selling has stopped, not capturing a fixed move. This directly confronts mean-reversion's structural failure mode: buying oversold in a name that is simply falling. Measured on the full 43-symbol universe through 2026-02-13 (RSI(14) crossing below 30, n=1990 signals over 8+ years), requiring close>sma(200) at signal (n=247) vs not (n=1743) raised the 10-day win rate from 55.3% to 61.1% and cut the average further adverse move over the next 10 days from -5.55% to -4.18% -- a real but modest effect, not a cure. Breaking that trend-filtered set down by symbol showed the semiconductor/AI-infrastructure cyclicals do not actually mean-revert even with the filter on: MU (n=8, mean 10d fwd -7.6%, 12.5% win), EWY (n=3, -8.6%, 0%), INTC (n=15, -2.9%, 40%), DELL (n=8, -2.8%, 37.5%), ORCL (n=13, -2.6%, 38.5%), NVDA (n=11, -0.4%, 54.5%) -- an oversold reading in these names was more often the first leg of a larger decline than a bounce, i.e. exactly the trap this discipline dies to, hiding inside a universe-level average that looked fine. I therefore excluded them. Eight names showed a genuine, if noisy, edge under the same filter: ADBE (n=14, +5.0%, 85.7% win), UNH (n=14, +5.3%, 64.3%), META (n=7, +5.5%, 71.4%), TSM (n=6, +4.6%, 83.3%), NFLX (n=10, +4.6%, 70%), GOOGL (n=14, +1.0%, 71.4%), QCOM (n=10, +1.4%, 60%), MSFT (n=11, +0.7%, 63.6%) -- combined 86 signals, mean 10-day forward return +3.4% (70.9% win), mean 20-day +4.0% (67.4% win), RSI(14) recovering above 50 within 20 sessions 72% of the time (median 9 sessions). Adverse excursion over the 20 sessions after entry: median -2.6%, 25th pct -6.7%, 10th pct -13.9%, 5th pct -17.8%; a 10% stop would have fired on ~16% of signals, catching the real washout-that-doesn't-turn tail without sitting inside the typical -3% to -7% pullback that produces the signal (mean washout depth from the trailing 20-day high at entry was -14.5%, so a tighter stop would fire on the setup itself). I also checked volatility comparability since the engine's stop_loss_pct/position_pct are single fixed numbers: trailing-120-day annualized return vol for the eight chosen names clusters 25.4%-40.9% (ATR/price 3.3%-4.7%), a ~1.6x band. I excluded SCHD/BRK.B (11.3%/13.6% ann vol) because a 10% stop is nearly unhittable there and their filtered signal count was thin (11, 16) anyway, and excluded AVGO/MRVL/AMD (49%-68% ann vol) because a 10% stop is closer to noise-width at that volatility, despite attractive-looking but tiny samples (n=3, 7, 12).
